newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brasilia awaits word on gov't shuffle in Congress.
newsitem.headline: Brasilia awaits word on gov't shuffle in Congress.

text.p: Brazilian political circles were on tenterhooks Monday, awaiting word of a possible reshuffle in the government's leadership in Congress.
President Fernando Henrique Cardoso spent nearly three hours talking with Luiz Eduardo Magalhaes, who has been tipped to take control of the government's floundering reform program.

A former president of the Chamber of Deputies who is considered one of the most dynamic figures in Congress, Magalhaes left the meeting in the presidential residence without speaking to reporters gathered at the gates outside.

Newspapers reported last week that Cardoso had offered Magalhaes the job of chief whip in Congress or in the Chamber of Deputies in the hope of finally getting his pension and civil service reform bills approved.

"Until we know how the political power balance has been changed, it's difficult to say exactly when we'll start voting again," said an aide to the government's leader in the lower house, Deputy Benito Gama, whose job Magalhaes might take.

The civil service reform bill was approved for a first time in the Chamber of Deputies nearly two months ago but wrangling among government-allied parties and an alleged corruption scandal have delayed voting on key amendments.

The pension reform bill was reported to be ready for presentation this week to a Senate committee. The government is hoping to rewrite the bill in the upper house to include key points which were lost during lower house voting last year. Once approved in the Senate, the bill will have to return to the Chamber of Deputies.

Officials say the government will press for approval of the reforms until September when its multi-party alliance of support in Congress is likely to dissolve in anticipation of the October 1998 presidential, state and congressional elections.

A more pressing issue is a bill extending the Fiscal Stabilization Fund (FEF), a key fiscal tool which allows the government to sidestep constitutional rules on spending and which is due to expire June 30.

A constitutional amendment to extend the fund for a further two-and-a-half years has yet to be approved in a lower house committee. It also requires two three-fifths majorities in the Chamber of Deputies and in the Senate.
The extension of the fund is reported to have run into resistance from several state governors and city mayors who stand to lose out from the fund's extension.

Less difficult should be a second and final approval in the Senate of a constitutional amendment allowing Cardoso, state governors and mayors to stand for re-election. The bill was approved for the first time last month by a wide margin and is expected to be approved again, probably Wednesday.
